context:
I have a smart-house sensor CSV and want a virtual meter: estimate appliance electricity
consumption in Wh for each ten-minute interval when the energy meter is unavailable. Sensors from
that same interval are available; this is estimation, not a future-weather forecast. Only room/building
temperature and humidity sensors (T1..T9, RH_1..RH_9) and calendar information are available inputs.
The lights meter and airport weather are unavailable inputs. Author metadata says rv1 and rv2 are
random noise controls. Future intervals should be held out chronologically. I care about errors and
systematic underestimation during evening hours 17..22, in addition to overall RMSE. This is a single
house: do not claim transfer to new buildings. Propose a suitable target, preparation and CPU models.
Available resources: CPU Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost and the new regularized linear models from the registry. Optional pretrained backends are unavailable for these runs. Choose any promising families from those choices; the simulated user will approve your proposed families once. The runtime includes an untuned constant fallback automatically, so you need not request it. You can compare multiple approved models in every trial, with bounded parallel CPU fits. Use standard preprocessing initially. Primary metric and target follow the objective above. At most five trials; use diagnostics, feature subsets, and model-specific parameters when justified.

insights: energy.csv is a single 19,735-row, 10-minute smart-house panel with no missing values; Appliances is a numeric Wh target with median 60, mean 97.7, and max 1080, suggesting right-skewed consumption that tree models can handle.
rv1 and rv2 have identical summary statistics and 19,735 unique values, consistent with random control columns; they should be excluded as non-informative noise.
lights, T_out, Press_mm_hg, RH_out, Windspeed, Visibility, and Tdewpoint are excluded because the objective restricts inputs to T1..T9/RH_1..RH_9 and calendar information.
A temporal holdout on date is appropriate because the virtual meter must estimate the same interval from contemporaneous sensors and future intervals must not leak into training.

Evening 17-22 underestimation is best monitored as a diagnostic residual bias by hour; adding hour and is_evening_17_22 features may help the model learn time-of-day patterns without changing the primary RMSE objective.
This is a single-house estimation task; results should not be interpreted as transferable to new buildings.
questions: Should evening 17-22 performance be a separate diagnostic, a weighted RMSE, or a hard constraint on underestimation?
Is Appliances the intended appliance-only target, or should lights be subtracted if the Appliances column includes lights?
Are T6 and RH_6 intended as indoor/building sensors, or should they be excluded if they represent outdoor conditions?
config.preparation: Use energy.csv as a single table with no joins. Parse date as datetime for temporal splitting and derive calendar features: hour, dayofweek, month, is_weekend, and is_evening_17_22. Target is Appliances. Exclude raw date, lights, T_out, Press_mm_hg, RH_out, Windspeed, Visibility, Tdewpoint, rv1, and rv2. Features are the 18 allowed sensor columns T1, RH_1, T2, RH_2, T3, RH_3, T4, RH_4, T5, RH_5, T6, RH_6, T7, RH_7, T8, RH_8, T9, RH_9 plus the derived calendar features. Use standard preprocessing and a temporal holdout on date; evaluate overall RMSE and diagnostic residual bias for hours 17-22.
config.rationale: Appliances is a defensible same-interval regression target for a virtual meter. The allowed inputs are contemporaneous room/building sensors and calendar features, so no lag or future-weather features are needed. A temporal split prevents leakage from future intervals. RMSE matches the stated overall error objective, while hour and is_evening_17_22 support diagnosing evening underestimation. Linear, random forest, LightGBM, and XGBoost provide a low-capacity control plus nonlinear CPU tabular models suitable for skewed, sensor-driven consumption.
